connector: Chapter 17 ended on January 1, 1863, with Harriet saying, “This is the first day we have ever had a country.” Now the Union army can fight for freedom out loud. In Chapter 18, General Hunter sends Harriet behind enemy lines. Collect the details Sterling chooses for the biggest night of her war.

a.raw: on a hot night in june three gunboats steamed up the combahee river
a.fixed: On a hot night in June three gunboats steamed up the Combahee River.
a.why: Capital O starts the sentence; capital J on June (a month); capital C and R on Combahee River (the name of a river); a period ends it. On a hot night, in June, and up the Combahee River are prepositional phrases.

b.raw: harriet crept through the underbrush past a rebel sentry
b.fixed: Harriet crept through the underbrush past a Rebel sentry.
b.why: Capital H on Harriet; capital R on Rebel, the way Sterling writes it; a period ends it. Through the underbrush and past a Rebel sentry are prepositional phrases that tell where.

fill1.h1: Trucks and ships carry things across. Which root means carry?
fill1.why: port means carry: trans + port + ation = carrying across.

fill2.h1: A volcano breaks open. Which root means break?
fill2.why: rupt means break: e + rupt = break out.

fill3.h1: Directions build up what you know. Which root means build?
fill3.why: struct means build: in + struct + ions = directions that build knowledge.

fill4.h1: To tell what will happen before it happens. Which root means say?
fill4.why: dict means say: pre + dict = say before.

notes.wordParts: port = carry, rupt = break, struct = build, dict = say: transport, erupt, instruct, predict.
notes.grammar: A prepositional phrase starts with a preposition (in, on, at, through, past, toward) and ends with a noun. It tells where, when, or how.
notes.spelling: Four suffix rules, one year: double the last consonant after a short vowel (run → running), drop the silent e (hope → hoping), and change y to i (happy → happiest, carry → carried). Look at the end of the base word first.

why.t: Harriet’s mother finished a patchwork quilt in Chapter 2, and all year the word-parts game has sewn patches like hers. This week it sews the last ones: four roots you met this year, port (carry), rupt (break), struct (build) and dict (say).

ft.songsIntro: On the Combahee River, the rowboats can’t push off. Everyone wants to get aboard at once, and frightened hands hold on to the sides. Colonel Montgomery shouts, “Moses, you’ll have to give ’em a song.”

songs.title: Come Along
lines: Of all the whole creation in the East or in the West,
The glorious Yankee nation is the greatest and the best.
Come along! Come along! Don’t be alarmed.
Uncle Sam is rich enough to give you all a farm.
songs.source: Harriet’s song on the Combahee, as Sterling gives it (Ch. 18, p. 172)
songs.heard: A bright, joking song about the Union and Uncle Sam, the nickname for the United States.
songs.meant: Don’t be afraid. You are welcome, and there is room for you. At the end of each verse the people threw up their hands and shouted, “Glory!”
songs.q: Why did Colonel Montgomery ask Harriet for a song?
songs.a: When the people let go of the boats to throw up their hands and shout “Glory!”, the rowers could push off. Load after load, almost eight hundred people got aboard.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Harriet is back in Union blue, and this time General Hunter needs her behind enemy lines. Chapter 18 is called Mr. Lincoln’s Army. It has the biggest night of her war. Today’s question: which details does Sterling choose to show you what that night meant?
transcripts.read: Track the details. A twig snaps near a Rebel sentry. Nine scouts learn where the torpedoes hide. Then three gunboats go up the Combahee River, and you’ll count the picket posts with Harriet. Watch the riverbanks at the end. On my tours, people always laughed about the two pigs.
transcripts.morphology: Last root review of the year. Port means carry. Rupt means break. Struct means build. Dict means say. They’ve been hiding in words all year. Ask what each word is doing: carrying, breaking, building, or saying. Then sew the patch.

virtue.title: Never in a better cause
virtue.intro: In Chapter 18, General Hunter warns Harriet about the penalty for spying. She answers, “I’ve faced death before, sir. But never in a better cause.” Then she guides three gunboats up the Combahee, and almost eight hundred people climb aboard the “Lincoln boats.”
virtue.line: Write one sentence: Why is freedom worth that risk to Harriet?
